candidate.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies → Adverse Effects/Biologic and Cellular Therapy: recognize severe treatment-related toxicity, provide urgent monitoring, differentiate competing causes, and prepare for prescribed rescue therapy.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — YESCARTA cytokine release syndrome recognition
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize fever, hypotension, and hypoxia after YESCARTA as possible cytokine release syndrome requiring urgent assessment, exclusion of alternative causes, and severity-based treatment preparation.

options.A: Suspect cytokine release syndrome, urgently escalate the findings, and evaluate for other causes of fever, hypotension, and hypoxia while preparing for severity-based prescribed treatment such as tocilizumab with or without corticosteroids.
options.B: Treat the findings as an expected harmless effect of CAR-T therapy because fever with hypotension and hypoxia does not require urgent assessment.
options.C: Conclude that the CAR-T treatment has failed because cytokine release syndrome occurs only when there is no therapeutic immune activity.
options.D: Assume infection is the only possible explanation and exclude CAR-T toxicity before any evaluation is performed.

candidate.rationale: Current YESCARTA prescribing information carries a boxed warning for cytokine release syndrome (CRS), including life-threatening and fatal reactions. Fever, hypotension, and hypoxia are characteristic manifestations used in CRS recognition and grading. The label instructs clinicians to identify CRS from the clinical presentation while also evaluating and treating other causes of fever, hypoxia, and hypotension. Severe or life-threatening CRS is treated with tocilizumab or tocilizumab plus corticosteroids according to severity. Therefore, A is correct. B dangerously normalizes a potentially fatal toxicity, C incorrectly equates CRS with treatment failure, and D prematurely excludes CAR-T toxicity rather than considering infection and other causes in the differential.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Directly supports recognition of post-YESCARTA fever, hypotension, and hypoxia as possible CRS, concurrent evaluation for alternative causes, urgent monitoring, and severity-based use of tocilizumab with or without corticosteroids.
candidate.source_locator: Boxed Warning and Section 5.1, Cytokine Release Syndrome: CRS including fatal/life-threatening reactions occurred after YESCARTA. Section 2.3, Management of Severe Adverse Reactions: identify CRS based on clinical presentation; evaluate for and treat other causes of fever, hypoxia, and hypotension; Grade 2 or higher CRS requires enhanced monitoring, and severe/life-threatening CRS may require intensive supportive care. Boxed Warning/Section 2.3: treat severe or life-threatening CRS with tocilizumab or tocilizumab and corticosteroids.
candidate.source_organization: National Library of Medicine / U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling via DailyMed
candidate.stem: Several days after receiving axicabtagene ciloleucel (YESCARTA), a client develops fever, hypotension, and new hypoxia. Which nursing interpretation is most appropriate?
